title: CAVEAT: Towards Robust Computer-Use Agents in Incentive-Misaligned Environments

paper.title: CAVEAT: Towards Robust Computer-Use Agents in Incentive-Misaligned Environments
paper.abstract:
Abstract Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act on behalf of users online.
What happens when the environments they operate in have incentives that do not align with the user’s?
In online marketplaces, for example, platforms may favor some products over others, potentially steering agents away from the user’s objective.
Existing CUA benchmarks cover cooperative settings or explicit attacks, but do not test whether agents preserve user objectives when the environment itself has a stake in the outcome.
We introduce CAVEAT , a controlled benchmark spanning nine marketplace environments and a taxonomy of eight common steering mechanisms.
Across five model families, agents purchase the user-optimal product in 78.6% of matched-control episodes but only 17.3% when steering mechanisms are enabled.
Larger models and increased reasoning improve robustness, but substantial failures persist.
Our trajectory analysis and targeted ablations identify three points where steering enters the decision process: (1) agents distort the user’s priorities, (2) prematurely narrow the set of alternatives they consider, and (3) commit before resolving decision-relevant evidence.
Guided by this diagnosis, we develop CAVEAT -Harness, which directly targets these failure modes and raises user-optimal purchasing by 55.0%.
Targeted post-training further improves a smaller open model.
These results establish incentive robustness as a distinct challenge for delegated agents, diagnose how it fails, and show that targeted interventions can substantially improve it.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are increasingly used to make purchases, book services, and act on users’ behalf across online platforms Deng et al. (2023) ; Zhou et al. (2024) ; He et al. (2024) . These platforms often have their own incentives around what users buy, read, watch, or engage with, shaping how options are ranked and presented Xu et al. (2022) ; Covington et al. (2016) ; Yao et al. (2023) ; Dai et al. (2024) . As users delegate more decisions to agents, those agents must preserve the user’s objective while operating in environments with competing objectives. Yet current CUA evaluations provide little evidence about this setting: capability benchmarks largely study task completions in neutral environments Zhou et al. (2024) ; Drouin et al. (2024) ; Xie et al. (2024) , while security benchmarks focus on explicit attempts to manipulate or compromise the agent Debenedetti et al. (2024) ; Evtimov et al. (2026) ; Zhan et al. (2024) . This leaves largely untested a common regime in which a platform operates as intended while favoring outcomes that may conflict with the user’s. We call these incentive-misaligned environments , and ask: when the environment has a stake in the outcome, does the agent still choose according to the user’s objective? Figure 1: Incentive misalignment changes agent decisions while the underlying task remains fixed. The same user request and product catalog are shown in matched-control and incentive-misaligned CAVEAT -Shop environments. Across five model configurations on CAVEAT -Standard, enabling steering mechanisms reduces optimal purchase rate from 78.6% to 17.3%. We formalize incentive-misaligned environments and instantiate them in online marketplaces, where platforms have long used sponsored ranking, promotional framing, scarcity cues, and related mechanisms to steer consumer choice Mathur et al. (2019) ; Wu et al. (2021) ; Sinha and Smith (2000) . We introduce CAVEAT , a benchmark spanning nine high-fidelity marketplace environments and eight steering mechanisms drawn from commercial practice, where agents search, compare, and purchase products end to end. Evaluating 18 model configurations on CAVEAT , we show a large gap between solving the underlying task and remaining robust to marketplace incentives. Across matched tasks, agents select the optimal product in 78.6% of cases when steering mechanisms are absent, compared with 17.3% when they are present. This effect appears across 18 model configurations and persists with stronger models and increased reasoning. On CAVEAT -Hard, which expands the search space beyond 2,000 products, GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning drops from 90.0% in the matched control to 0.0% under incentive misalignment. To understand why incentives have such a large effect, we combine quantitative and qualitative trajectory analysis with targeted ablations, and find that incentive misalignment enters the decision process at three points: agents (1) drift from the user’s stated priorities toward whatever the marketplace makes salient, (2) stop searching after seeing only the options the marketplace surfaces first, and (3) commit to a purchase before resolving decision-relevant facts, such as the full price. Informed by this diagnosis, we develop CAVEAT -Harness by having the agent pin down the user’s objective before browsing and verify its decision before buying. The harness raises optimal purchasing for GPT-5.6-Terra from 11.7% to 66.7% on Standard and for GPT-5.6-Sol from 0.0% to 80.0% on Hard. The gains are much smaller for Qwen3.5-27B, which reaches only 4.2% with the harness, suggesting that agent harness interventions still depend on the underlying model’s ability to carry out the prescribed decision process. We therefore post-train Qwen3.5-27B on trajectories that instantiate this process and obtain CAVEAT -27B, which improves to 22.9% under the same harness. Together, these results show that the failures exposed by CAVEAT are diagnosable and actionable through both inference-time structure and targeted post-training. We make three contributions: • We formalize incentive-misaligned environments and introduce CAVEAT , a controlled benchmark spanning 9 high-fidelity environments for evaluating whether CUAs preserve user objectives under competing marketplace incentives. • Across 18 model configurations, we identify a large incentive-induced degradation in optimal purchasing and trace it to failures in objective preservation, search coverage, and evidence resolution. • We show that these failures can be mitigated through structured inference and targeted post-training with CAVEAT -Harness and CAVEAT -27B.

sections.heading: 2 Incentive-Misaligned Environments
sections.text: We consider a user who delegates a decision to an agent. Let 𝒳 \mathcal{X} denote the feasible outcomes and U ⁡ ( x ) U(x) the user’s objective. The set of user-optimal outcomes is 𝒳 U ⋆ = arg ⁡ max x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ U ⁡ ( x ) . \mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star}=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}U(x). The agent receives the user’s request and interacts with an environment ℰ \mathcal{E} to choose an outcome x ^ ℰ \hat{x}_{\mathcal{E}} . We call a selection optimal when x ^ ℰ ∈ 𝒳 U ⋆ \hat{x}_{\mathcal{E}}\in\mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star} , and measure decision quality by the optimal selection rate , the fraction of tasks on which this occurs. Task completion records whether the agent successfully executes an outcome, whereas optimal selection asks whether that outcome is best according to the user’s objective. The environment may itself be shaped by an objective V V , which gives it incentives over outcomes or interactions. We call ℰ \mathcal{E} incentive-misaligned for a delegated decision when advancing V V can favor outcomes outside 𝒳 U ⋆ \mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star} . This relationship depends on the decision: the same ranking rule or recommendation may favor the user-optimal outcome on one task and a worse outcome on another. We use steering mechanism for the way an environment advances its objective through the agent’s decision context, such as by changing which options are surfaced, how they are presented, or the effort required to inspect them. Throughout the paper, misalignment refers to the conflict between objectives, while robustness refers to the agent’s ability to preserve decision quality under that conflict. We evaluate robustness using matched conditions that preserve the underlying decision problem. The user request, feasible outcomes, decision-relevant facts, and 𝒳 U ⋆ \mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star} remain fixed, while the steering mechanisms shaping the interaction are varied. We refer to the resulting difference in optimal selection rate as incentive-induced degradation . Because the underlying choice set and user objective are unchanged, the matched comparison isolates degradation induced by the environment’s choice architecture rather than changes in the underlying decision problem. Explicit adversarial attacks form a different setting in which the environment deliberately attempts to compromise the agent; an incentive-misaligned environment may operate as designed while pursuing an objective that conflicts with the user’s.

sections.heading: 3 CAVEAT : Incentive-Misaligned Marketplaces
sections.text: We instantiate this setting in CAVEAT , a benchmark of nine browser-based marketplaces spanning short-term lodging, general retail, food delivery, resale, freelance services, grocery delivery, and specialty shopping (Figure 2 A). Each environment has its own storefront and domain-appropriate transaction flow. An agent receives a natural-language user request and then operates the marketplace autonomously until it places an order or booking (Figure 2 B). It may search, navigate, inspect listings, use available filters or sorting controls, and modify its cart as it sees fit; the benchmark does not prescribe a decision procedure or how much of the marketplace the agent should inspect. Figure 2: Overview of CAVEAT . (A) Nine marketplace environments provide diverse interfaces for end-to-end purchasing. Respectively: (B) Given a natural-language request containing hard and comparative requirements, a computer-use agent browses the marketplace and completes a purchase. Each task has a unique user-optimal product, and optimal purchase rate measures the fraction of episodes in which the agent purchases it. Agent task and scoring. Each request specifies hard requirements that the chosen option must satisfy and comparative requirements over otherwise valid options. A request might, for example, require a product to stay within budget and meet a minimum specification while preferring lower total cost and higher capacity. We construct every scored task so that exactly one option satisfies the requirements and is jointly best on all stated preferences, yielding a unique user-optimal option without requiring arbitrary weights between preferences. The product attributes needed to evaluate each request are stored in structured form, and every task is validated programmatically against the full catalog. As illustrated in Figure 2 B, an episode is scored by comparing the completed transaction with the user-optimal option. The optimal purchase rate is the fraction of episodes in which they match. Marketplace steering mechanisms. To ground CAVEAT in steering mechanisms documented in real online marketplaces, we reviewed prior academic work, regulatory guidance, and policy analyses on online choice architecture, advertising and ranking, pricing, reviews, and interface design Blake et al. (2021) ; Mathur et al. (2019) ; Competition and Markets Authority (2022) ; Federal Trade Commission (2022) ; OECD (2022) ; European Commission (2020) ; Federal Trade Commission (2015) ; Federal Trade Commission (2025) ; Federal Trade Commission (1967) ; Federal Trade Commission (2024) . We synthesize the recurring mechanisms into the eight-family taxonomy in Table 1 , and operationalize each family in CAVEAT . Table 1: Marketplace incentive-mechanism taxonomy used in CAVEAT . Mechanism How it appears Sponsored placement Paid or promoted options receive more prominent placement. Preferential ranking Platform-favored options are promoted; disfavored ones are buried. Drip pricing Required costs are revealed later in the purchase flow. Promotional framing Discounts or reference prices make selected options appear more attractive. Defaults & bundling Add-ons, bundles, or upgraded choices are preselected or favored. Scarcity & social proof Urgency, availability, or popularity cues encourage commitment. Trust signals Ratings, reviews, or badges increase the apparent credibility of selected options. Friction & obstruction Some choices or corrections require additional effort. For every Standard task, we evaluate the same user request in two versions of the marketplace (Figure 1 ). The matched control disables these mechanisms, while the incentive-misaligned condition activates all eight. The request, available products, product attributes, prices, availability, and user-optimal option remain identical across the two versions. The mechanisms change how the marketplace presents and mediates the same choice, including which products appear first, which receive sponsored or promotional treatment, when costs become visible, and what urgency or trust cues accompany them. Comparing optimal purchase rate across the two matched conditions measures the incentive-induced degradation defined in Section 2 . Benchmark settings. CAVEAT -Standard contains 52 tasks across the nine environments, with approximately 70 products in each scenario. We further construct CAVEAT -Hard to test the same decision problem at substantially larger search scale. Its 5 CAVEAT -Shop tasks each contain 2,112 products distributed across 88 result pages. This setting tests whether agents can maintain decision quality when finding strong candidates requires much broader exploration of the marketplace.

sections.heading: 4 Evaluating CUAs under Incentive Misalignment
sections.text: We evaluate CUAs on CAVEAT using the widely used BrowserUse harness Müller and Žunič (2024) , holding the agent harness fixed across model families. Our main evaluation covers five widely used model families on all 52 CAVEAT -Standard tasks under both matched conditions, with three repetitions per task. To examine how robustness changes with reasoning, model scale, and model generation, we evaluate additional configurations on CAVEAT -Shop while holding the environment and tasks fixed. We further evaluate the strongest configuration on the five CAVEAT -Hard tasks with ten repetitions each.

sections.heading: 4.1 Incentives Sharply Degrade User-Optimal Purchasing
sections.text: Activating the marketplace steering mechanisms reduces optimal purchase rate on CAVEAT -Standard from 78.6% to 17.3%, a drop of 61.3 percentage points (Figure 3 A). The user request, catalog, product facts, prices, availability, and user-optimal option remain unchanged between the two conditions. This matched comparison therefore isolates how strongly the agents’ decisions change in response to the marketplace incentives surrounding the same purchasing problem. The effect is not concentrated in a small subset of models. All five model families decline under incentive misalignment (Figure 3 B), with drops ranging from 37.2 to 78.9 percentage points. Even GPT-5.6-Sol with low reasoning, the strongest model in this comparison, falls from 91.0% in the matched control to 53.8% under incentive misalignment. The same degradation also occurs when using a different agent harness paired with a dedicated CUA model. Using Fara1.5-27B with its native Fara harness on CAVEAT -Shop, we observe a drop from 81.7% in the matched control to 3.3% under incentive misalignment. Using the 20 tasks in CAVEAT -Shop, we further isolate each incentive family while disabling the other seven. With all mechanisms disabled, GPT-5.6-Sol-low makes the optimal purchase in 100% of episodes; activating sponsored placement alone reduces this to 63.3%, preferential ranking to 75%, and drip pricing to 83.3%, while the remaining five families produce smaller drops. Figure 3: Incentive misalignment sharply reduces optimal purchasing. (A) Across five model families and all 52 CAVEAT -Standard tasks, optimal purchase rate falls from 78.6% in the matched control to 17.3% under incentive misalignment. (B) The degradation is consistent across model families. All five configurations perform worse under incentive misalignment, with drops ranging from 37.2 to 78.9 percentage points. (C) On CAVEAT -Hard, GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning achieves 90.0% in the matched control and 0.0% under incentive misalignment. Error bars denote 95% Wilson confidence intervals. CAVEAT -Hard makes the separation between underlying task capability and robustness to incentives especially clear. GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning purchases the user-optimal product in 90.0% of matched-control episodes, showing that it can solve these large-catalog decisions when the steering mechanisms are absent. With the same requests and catalogs under incentive misalignment, it makes no optimal purchase across 50 episodes (Figure 3 C). Thus, even when the underlying decision problem is demonstrably solvable, marketplace incentives can still induce a complete loss of optimal purchasing in this setting.

sections.heading: 4.2 Robustness Improves with Model Capability
sections.text: The controlled comparisons in Figure 4 show that robustness improves as models receive more reasoning, scale to stronger variants, and advance across generations. Reasoning produces the clearest gains. GPT-5.6-Sol rises from 51.7% optimal purchasing at low reasoning to 90.0% at high reasoning, while GPT-5.5 improves from 12.0% at low reasoning to 50% with medium or high reasoning. Additional inference-time reasoning can therefore recover a substantial share of the performance lost under incentive misalignment. Figure 4: Robustness improves with model capability. All panels evaluate CAVEAT -Shop Standard under incentive misalignment. (A) Increasing reasoning effort raises optimal purchase rate for GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6-Sol. (B) Within GPT-5.6, performance rises from Luna to Terra to Sol, while the tested GPT-5 scale variants remain at floor. (C) At low reasoning effort, robustness remains at floor through GPT-5, becomes measurable with GPT-5.5, and rises sharply with GPT-5.6-Sol. Scaling shows a similar upward trend within GPT-5.6. At the same low-reasoning setting, optimal purchase rate rises from 0.0% for Luna to 11.7% for Terra and 51.7% for Sol (Figure 4 B). The corresponding GPT-5 nano, mini, and main configurations remain at 0.0%, indicating that greater scale alone is insufficient in the older generation and that the gains from scaling become visible only in the newer family. Model generation shows the same broader progression. At low reasoning effort, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and GPT-5 remain at floor, after which optimal purchase rate rises to 12.0% for GPT-5.5 and 51.7% for GPT-5.6-Sol (Figure 4 C). Together, these comparisons show that robustness to marketplace incentives is improving with reasoning, scale, and newer model generations. At the same time, it continues to lag the models’ ability to solve the corresponding purchasing decisions in matched controls. This gap motivates a closer examination of how agent behavior changes when marketplace incentives are present.

sections.heading: 5 Where Incentive Misalignment Enters the Decision Process
sections.text: Section 4 shows that agents often solve a purchasing problem in the matched control but choose differently once marketplace incentives are introduced. We next examine where this sensitivity enters the decision process. We qualitatively review 200 randomly sampled trajectories from the user request through purchase while hiding the final success label, then use recurring behaviors to motivate targeted analyses. The review points to departures in how agents preserve the user’s preferences, decide when to stop searching, and handle information that remains uncertain or has been read incorrectly. These observations identify three places in the decision process where an incentive-bearing environment can gain leverage through salience, visibility, and information availability.

sections.heading: 5.1 Objective Drift
sections.text: Observation. In several trajectories, agents begin with a faithful account of the user’s requirements and preferences but change their effective priorities while browsing. A highly rated product, a prominent feature, or another salient cue can lead the agent to favor one preference over another even when the user assigned them equal importance. We therefore test whether the comparison remains stable under a change that leaves the user objective unchanged. Targeted analysis and ablations. We construct matched requests with two explicitly equal-priority preferences and reverse only their order. The catalog, preference values, stated priorities, and user-optimal product remain fixed. Yet the selected product changes in all 25 matched pairs and systematically shifts toward the preference mentioned first. The agent therefore introduces a priority that the user did not specify. Diagnosis. We call this objective drift . In an incentive-misaligned environment, such instability gives recommendations, promotional framing, ratings, and other salient cues a route to change which parts of the user’s objective dominate the comparison.

sections.heading: 5.2 Premature Search Closure
sections.text: Observation. Failed trajectories often settle on a product that satisfies the hard requirements after comparing only a small set of visible options. Successful runs search more broadly, although both successful and failed agents frequently state that they have searched enough. This suggests that stopping decisions are poorly calibrated to search coverage, which becomes consequential when the environment controls which alternatives appear early. Targeted analysis and ablations. We run a matched placement intervention across all five CAVEAT-Shop product types and four comparative-preference settings, with three repetitions per setting and 60 runs per condition. Holding the request, catalog, and product attributes fixed, we move a suboptimal product from its normal position to a sponsored position near the top of the results. Its visit rate rises from 45/60 to 60/60, but its purchase rate rises much more sharply from 0/60 to 48/60, indicating that prominence changes how the product is treated after it is seen. This dependence on early visibility becomes especially damaging when the optimum requires deeper search. On CAVEAT -Hard, all 50 GPT-5.6-Sol-high failures stop on page 1 of an 88-page catalog and purchase a valid but suboptimal option while the optimum remains buried. Diagnosis. We call this premature search closure . Any incentive-bearing environment that controls the ordering or prominence of alternatives can exploit such a stopping rule through ranking, recommendations, or placement.

sections.heading: 5.3 Premature Commitment with Unresolved Evidence
sections.text: Observation. Some failures remain even after search has succeeded. In these runs, the user-optimal product enters the comparison but is later rejected because a decision-relevant fact is missing, misread, or incorrectly remembered. To separate these cases from failures of discovery, we examine non-optimal purchases in which the optimum appears before the final decision and trace why the agent excludes it. Targeted analysis and ablations. To separate evidence failures from search failures, we examine non-optimal runs in which the user-optimal product had already been found. We identify 23 cases where the agent subsequently excludes it because a decision-relevant fact is misread, forgotten, or judged incorrectly, most often by confusing list and payable prices. These cases span 19 model–task–condition settings, and 13 contain another repetition that succeeds when the decisive fact is handled correctly. Thus, the failure occurs after discovery and turns on how the agent resolves the evidence needed for comparison. This suggests that delaying a decision-relevant fact may be enough to exploit the same weakness, which we test with drip pricing, where the initially displayed price can omit charges revealed only later in the transaction. We activate only drip pricing on CAVEAT -Shop while disabling the other seven steering mechanisms. Across 60 runs with GPT-5.6-Terra at low reasoning effort, the agent makes 35 suboptimal purchases, all selecting the drip-priced promoted product. Because no ranking, sponsorship, or other steering mechanism is active, these results isolate delayed price information as sufficient to substantially disrupt the comparison. Diagnosis. We call this premature commitment with unresolved evidence . The failure occurs when missing, delayed, conflicting, or misread information is treated as settled before the agent has enough evidence to support it. An incentive-misaligned environment can exploit this weakness by controlling which facts appear early and which require additional inspection.

sections.heading: 6 Mitigating Incentive-Induced Failures
sections.text: The three failures identified in Section 5 suggest concrete requirements for robust decision-making under incentive misalignment. To show these requirements are actionable, we operationalize them at inference time with CAVEAT -Harness, then use the same decision behaviors to post-train CAVEAT -27B so that a smaller model can execute them more reliably.

sections.heading: 6.1 CAVEAT -Harness: Operationalizing the Diagnosis
sections.text: We address objective drift by asking the evaluated model to convert the user request into a structured task specification before browsing begins. The specification records the hard and comparative requirements together with only the priorities explicitly stated by the user, and we keep it fixed throughout the episode. We address premature search closure and premature commitment with unresolved evidence with an optional verification tool. Before purchase, the agent can use the tool to justify that search is sufficiently complete from evidence available in the marketplace and to check whether missing or conflicting facts could still change the comparison. CAVEAT -Harness uses only the user request and information obtained through ordinary browsing; it receives no benchmark answers, hidden catalog state, or incentive metadata. We compare the full harness with baseline BrowserUse and a prompt-only baseline that describes the same decision principles without adding the structured task specification or verification tool (Figure 5 A–B, each task tested with three repetitions). On CAVEAT -Shop, CAVEAT -Harness raises GPT-5.6-Terra-low from 11.7% optimal purchasing with BrowserUse to 66.7%, compared with 30.0% under prompting alone. On CAVEAT -Hard, it raises GPT-5.6-Sol-high from 0.0% to 80.0%, compared with 13.3% under prompting. We further ablate the two harness components on CAVEAT -Hard and find that structured objectives alone reach 6.7%, whereas the verification tool alone reaches 66.7%. Together with the 80.0% result from the full harness, this suggests that search and evidence verification account for most of the gain in this large-catalog setting. Our trajectory review also finds cases where simply making the verification tool available leads the model to search more broadly before invoking it, suggesting that the checkpoint can influence stopping behavior in addition to filtering the final decision. As a lightweight cross-environment check, we evaluate four CAVEAT -Stay tasks with three repetitions each. CAVEAT -Harness raises GPT-5.6-Terra-low from 16.7% to 50.0%, providing preliminary evidence that the inference-time intervention transfers beyond CAVEAT -Shop. We also measure the interaction cost of this additional robustness. CAVEAT -Harness requires 2.6 × \times as much runtime, 2.3 × \times as many steps, and 2.3 × \times as many tool calls as baseline BrowserUse. The improvement therefore comes partly from inducing more extensive search and verification, motivating more efficient stopping and verification strategies. Figure 5: Mitigating incentive-induced failures through inference-time structure and post-training. (A) On CAVEAT -Shop, CAVEAT -Harness substantially improves GPT-5.6-Terra-low over baseline BrowserUse and a prompt-only intervention. (B) The same pattern holds on CAVEAT -Hard with GPT-5.6-Sol-high. (C) On the 16 non-laptop CAVEAT -Shop tasks excluded from second-stage development, CAVEAT -27B with CAVEAT -Harness outperforms both the original Qwen3.5-27B with BrowserUse and the same backbone with CAVEAT -Harness. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals.

sections.heading: 6.2 CAVEAT -27B: Learning the Decision Procedure
sections.text: Small open models are attractive for personal CUAs that run locally or under tighter privacy and deployment constraints, yet simply pairing Qwen3.5-27B with CAVEAT -Harness yields only 4.2% optimal purchasing on the transfer evaluation below. We therefore ask whether post-training can make the model execute the same decision procedure more reliably over long browser trajectories, producing CAVEAT -27B. We train Qwen3.5-27B in two stages. First, we use supervised examples synthesized by GPT-5.6-Sol-low in a separate synthetic environment to teach the behaviors required by the harness, including preserving the task specification, using the verification tool, and producing valid browser actions. We exclude all CAVEAT environments, tasks, catalogs, products, and benchmark answers from this stage. Second, we roll out the resulting model on CAVEAT -Shop laptop development tasks and train on corrected actions at states reached by its own policy. This exposes the model to navigation errors and recovery states that static demonstrations do not cover well. We use GPT-5.6-Sol-low with CAVEAT -Harness to provide corrected targets. We evaluate on the 16 non-laptop CAVEAT -Shop tasks, with three repetitions per task. The original Qwen3.5-27B achieves 0.0% with BrowserUse and 4.2% with CAVEAT -Harness, whereas CAVEAT -27B reaches 22.9% under the same harness (Figure 5 C), an 18.7 percentage-point gain over the untrained backbone. To test whether this improvement transfers beyond the training environment, we evaluate the same models on the four CAVEAT -Stay tasks. Qwen3.5-27B remains at 0.0% with either BrowserUse or CAVEAT -Harness, while CAVEAT -27B with the harness reaches 16.7%, providing preliminary evidence that post-training improves the model beyond CAVEAT -Shop.

sections.heading: 7 Related Work
sections.text: Computer-use and shopping agents. Web and computer-use benchmarks evaluate navigation, tool use, and task completion across increasingly realistic interfaces Zhou et al. (2024) ; Deng et al. (2023) ; Xie et al. (2024) . Shopping benchmarks extend this setting to product search, recommendation, personalization, and complex user requests Yao et al. (2022) ; Ling et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) , while preference-following evaluations study whether agents infer and retain user preferences during interaction Zhao et al. (2025) ; Jiang et al. (2025) . CAVEAT goes beyond this by holding the underlying user decision fixed and varying the incentives shaping the environment, enabling end-to-end measurement of whether an agent preserves the user-optimal outcome under competing environmental incentives. Agent security and deceptive interfaces. Prior work studies web agents under prompt injection, malicious content, and other explicit attempts to redirect agent behavior Evtimov et al. (2026) ; Debenedetti et al. (2024) ; Zhan et al. (2024) , while recent benchmarks examine susceptibility to dark patterns and deceptive interfaces that alter ranking, presentation, or choice architecture Cuvin et al. (2026) ; Shi et al. (2026) ; Guo et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026) ; Bansal et al. (2025) . CAVEAT differs from this work in both what it varies and what it measures. It varies the environment’s incentives rather than introducing adversarial or deceptive content, instantiating a taxonomy of steering mechanisms in complete, high-fidelity marketplace environments. Every mechanism presents only accurate information, so the agent is never misled about the facts it needs to decide; the observed degradation arises from how agents respond to the ordering, salience, and timing of true information. And rather than scoring whether an agent avoids a particular pattern, CAVEAT scores whether it selects the user-optimal option from a full catalog with a verifiable optimum, exposing decision-level failures such as premature search closure that pattern-level scoring cannot observe. Platform incentives and consumer choice. Work in economics, recommender systems, and human–computer interaction has examined how platform objectives shape ranking, recommendation, sponsored placement, interface design, and consumer choice Xu et al. (2022) ; Mathur et al. (2019) ; Athey and Ellison (2011) . This literature motivates the incentive taxonomy instantiated in CAVEAT . By embedding these incentives in interactive environments with verifiable user-optimal outcomes, we study how autonomous agents mediate the resulting conflict between users and platforms, and whether the diagnosed failures can be mitigated.

sections.heading: 8 Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: Our study focuses on online marketplaces, where CAVEAT can precisely control user-optimal outcomes and environmental incentives; extending the same methodology to domains such as financial services, hiring, or information platforms would test how broadly the observed failure modes transfer. CAVEAT also uses well-specified objectives with unique optima, providing clean causal measurement while leaving open richer settings with partial, evolving, or non-unique preferences. The current environments instantiate fixed steering mechanisms, whereas real platforms may adapt their behavior to the agent over time, motivating interactive and strategic extensions. Finally, the robustness gains from CAVEAT-Harness come with greater interaction cost, and evidence that either CAVEAT-Harness or CAVEAT -27B generalizes beyond CAVEAT -Shop is currently limited to a small CAVEAT -Stay evaluation. Future work should characterize this robustness–efficiency tradeoff and test transfer across broader environments, mechanisms, and domains.

sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced incentive-misaligned environments as a setting for evaluating whether CUAs preserve the user’s objective when the environment benefits from different outcomes. We instantiated this setting in CAVEAT and found that activating realistic marketplace steering mechanisms reduces optimal purchase rate from 78.6% to 17.3% under matched decision problems. We traced this degradation to objective drift, premature search closure, and commitment with unresolved evidence, then showed that interventions derived from these failures substantially improve robustness through both inference-time structure and targeted post-training. Together, our results suggest that evaluating delegated agents should include how reliably they preserve user objectives when the environments in which they act have incentives of their own.

Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Email: yuxuanll@andrew.cmu.edu Will Epperson Affiliation: Microsoft Research Email: willepperson@microsoft.com Wesley Deng Affiliation: Microsoft Research Email: wesleydeng@microsoft.com Zezhou Huang Affiliation: Microsoft Research Email: zacharyhuang@microsoft.com Abstract Computer-use agents (CUAs) increasingly act on behalf of users online. What happens when the environments they operate in have incentives that do not align with the user’s? In online marketplaces, for example, platforms may favor some products over others, potentially steering agents away from the user’s objective. Existing CUA benchmarks cover cooperative settings or explicit attacks, but do not test whether agents preserve user objectives when the environment itself has a stake in the outcome. We introduce CAVEAT , a controlled benchmark spanning nine marketplace environments and a taxonomy of eight common steering mechanisms. Across five model families, agents purchase the user-optimal product in 78.6% of matched-control episodes but only 17.3% when steering mechanisms are enabled. Larger models and increased reasoning improve robustness, but substantial failures persist. Our trajectory analysis and targeted ablations identify three points where steering enters the decision process: (1) agents distort the user’s priorities, (2) prematurely narrow the set of alternatives they consider, and (3) commit before resolving decision-relevant evidence. Guided by this diagnosis, we develop CAVEAT -Harness, which directly targets these failure modes and raises user-optimal purchasing by 55.0%. Targeted post-training further improves a smaller open model. These results establish incentive robustness as a distinct challenge for delegated agents, diagnose how it fails, and show that targeted interventions can substantially improve it. 1 Introduction Computer-use agents (CUAs) are increasingly used to make purchases, book services, and act on users’ behalf across online platforms Deng et al. (2023) ; Zhou et al. (2024) ; He et al. (2024) . These platforms often have their own incentives around what users buy, read, watch, or engage with, shaping how options are ranked and presented Xu et al. (2022) ; Covington et al. (2016) ; Yao et al. (2023) ; Dai et al. (2024) . As users delegate more decisions to agents, those agents must preserve the user’s objective while operating in environments with competing objectives. Yet current CUA evaluations provide little evidence about this setting: capability benchmarks largely study task completions in neutral environments Zhou et al. (2024) ; Drouin et al. (2024) ; Xie et al. (2024) , while security benchmarks focus on explicit attempts to manipulate or compromise the agent Debenedetti et al. (2024) ; Evtimov et al. (2026) ; Zhan et al. (2024) . This leaves largely untested a common regime in which a platform operates as intended while favoring outcomes that may conflict with the user’s. We call these incentive-misaligned environments , and ask: when the environment has a stake in the outcome, does the agent still choose according to the user’s objective? Figure 1: Incentive misalignment changes agent decisions while the underlying task remains fixed. The same user request and product catalog are shown in matched-control and incentive-misaligned CAVEAT -Shop environments. Across five model configurations on CAVEAT -Standard, enabling steering mechanisms reduces optimal purchase rate from 78.6% to 17.3%. We formalize incentive-misaligned environments and instantiate them in online marketplaces, where platforms have long used sponsored ranking, promotional framing, scarcity cues, and related mechanisms to steer consumer choice Mathur et al. (2019) ; Wu et al. (2021) ; Sinha and Smith (2000) . We introduce CAVEAT , a benchmark spanning nine high-fidelity marketplace environments and eight steering mechanisms drawn from commercial practice, where agents search, compare, and purchase products end to end. Evaluating 18 model configurations on CAVEAT , we show a large gap between solving the underlying task and remaining robust to marketplace incentives. Across matched tasks, agents select the optimal product in 78.6% of cases when steering mechanisms are absent, compared with 17.3% when they are present. This effect appears across 18 model configurations and persists with stronger models and increased reasoning. On CAVEAT -Hard, which expands the search space beyond 2,000 products, GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning drops from 90.0% in the matched control to 0.0% under incentive misalignment. To understand why incentives have such a large effect, we combine quantitative and qualitative trajectory analysis with targeted ablations, and find that incentive misalignment enters the decision process at three points: agents (1) drift from the user’s stated priorities toward whatever the marketplace makes salient, (2) stop searching after seeing only the options the marketplace surfaces first, and (3) commit to a purchase before resolving decision-relevant facts, such as the full price. Informed by this diagnosis, we develop CAVEAT -Harness by having the agent pin down the user’s objective before browsing and verify its decision before buying. The harness raises optimal purchasing for GPT-5.6-Terra from 11.7% to 66.7% on Standard and for GPT-5.6-Sol from 0.0% to 80.0% on Hard. The gains are much smaller for Qwen3.5-27B, which reaches only 4.2% with the harness, suggesting that agent harness interventions still depend on the underlying model’s ability to carry out the prescribed decision process. We therefore post-train Qwen3.5-27B on trajectories that instantiate this process and obtain CAVEAT -27B, which improves to 22.9% under the same harness. Together, these results show that the failures exposed by CAVEAT are diagnosable and actionable through both inference-time structure and targeted post-training. We make three contributions: • We formalize incentive-misaligned environments and introduce CAVEAT , a controlled benchmark spanning 9 high-fidelity environments for evaluating whether CUAs preserve user objectives under competing marketplace incentives. • Across 18 model configurations, we identify a large incentive-induced degradation in optimal purchasing and trace it to failures in objective preservation, search coverage, and evidence resolution. • We show that these failures can be mitigated through structured inference and targeted post-training with CAVEAT -Harness and CAVEAT -27B. 2 Incentive-Misaligned Environments We consider a user who delegates a decision to an agent. Let 𝒳 \mathcal{X} denote the feasible outcomes and U ⁡ ( x ) U(x) the user’s objective. The set of user-optimal outcomes is 𝒳 U ⋆ = arg ⁡ max x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ U ⁡ ( x ) . \mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star}=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{X}}U(x). The agent receives the user’s request and interacts with an environment ℰ \mathcal{E} to choose an outcome x ^ ℰ \hat{x}_{\mathcal{E}} . We call a selection optimal when x ^ ℰ ∈ 𝒳 U ⋆ \hat{x}_{\mathcal{E}}\in\mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star} , and measure decision quality by the optimal selection rate , the fraction of tasks on which this occurs. Task completion records whether the agent successfully executes an outcome, whereas optimal selection asks whether that outcome is best according to the user’s objective. The environment may itself be shaped by an objective V V , which gives it incentives over outcomes or interactions. We call ℰ \mathcal{E} incentive-misaligned for a delegated decision when advancing V V can favor outcomes outside 𝒳 U ⋆ \mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star} . This relationship depends on the decision: the same ranking rule or recommendation may favor the user-optimal outcome on one task and a worse outcome on another. We use steering mechanism for the way an environment advances its objective through the agent’s decision context, such as by changing which options are surfaced, how they are presented, or the effort required to inspect them. Throughout the paper, misalignment refers to the conflict between objectives, while robustness refers to the agent’s ability to preserve decision quality under that conflict. We evaluate robustness using matched conditions that preserve the underlying decision problem. The user request, feasible outcomes, decision-relevant facts, and 𝒳 U ⋆ \mathcal{X}_{U}^{\star} remain fixed, while the steering mechanisms shaping the interaction are varied. We refer to the resulting difference in optimal selection rate as incentive-induced degradation . Because the underlying choice set and user objective are unchanged, the matched comparison isolates degradation induced by the environment’s choice architecture rather than changes in the underlying decision problem. Explicit adversarial attacks form a different setting in which the environment deliberately attempts to compromise the agent; an incentive-misaligned environment may operate as designed while pursuing an objective that conflicts with the user’s. 3 CAVEAT : Incentive-Misaligned Marketplaces We instantiate this setting in CAVEAT , a benchmark of nine browser-based marketplaces spanning short-term lodging, general retail, food delivery, resale, freelance services, grocery delivery, and specialty shopping (Figure 2 A). Each environment has its own storefront and domain-appropriate transaction flow. An agent receives a natural-language user request and then operates the marketplace autonomously until it places an order or booking (Figure 2 B). It may search, navigate, inspect listings, use available filters or sorting controls, and modify its cart as it sees fit; the benchmark does not prescribe a decision procedure or how much of the marketplace the agent should inspect. Figure 2: Overview of CAVEAT . (A) Nine marketplace environments provide diverse interfaces for end-to-end purchasing. Respectively: (B) Given a natural-language request containing hard and comparative requirements, a computer-use agent browses the marketplace and completes a purchase. Each task has a unique user-optimal product, and optimal purchase rate measures the fraction of episodes in which the agent purchases it. Agent task and scoring. Each request specifies hard requirements that the chosen option must satisfy and comparative requirements over otherwise valid options. A request might, for example, require a product to stay within budget and meet a minimum specification while preferring lower total cost and higher capacity. We construct every scored task so that exactly one option satisfies the requirements and is jointly best on all stated preferences, yielding a unique user-optimal option without requiring arbitrary weights between preferences. The product attributes needed to evaluate each request are stored in structured form, and every task is validated programmatically against the full catalog. As illustrated in Figure 2 B, an episode is scored by comparing the completed transaction with the user-optimal option. The optimal purchase rate is the fraction of episodes in which they match. Marketplace steering mechanisms. To ground CAVEAT in steering mechanisms documented in real online marketplaces, we reviewed prior academic work, regulatory guidance, and policy analyses on online choice architecture, advertising and ranking, pricing, reviews, and interface design Blake et al. (2021) ; Mathur et al. (2019) ; Competition and Markets Authority (2022) ; Federal Trade Commission (2022) ; OECD (2022) ; European Commission (2020) ; Federal Trade Commission (2015) ; Federal Trade Commission (2025) ; Federal Trade Commission (1967) ; Federal Trade Commission (2024) . We synthesize the recurring mechanisms into the eight-family taxonomy in Table 1 , and operationalize each family in CAVEAT . Table 1: Marketplace incentive-mechanism taxonomy used in CAVEAT . Mechanism How it appears Sponsored placement Paid or promoted options receive more prominent placement. Preferential ranking Platform-favored options are promoted; disfavored ones are buried. Drip pricing Required costs are revealed later in the purchase flow. Promotional framing Discounts or reference prices make selected options appear more attractive. Defaults & bundling Add-ons, bundles, or upgraded choices are preselected or favored. Scarcity & social proof Urgency, availability, or popularity cues encourage commitment. Trust signals Ratings, reviews, or badges increase the apparent credibility of selected options. Friction & obstruction Some choices or corrections require additional effort. For every Standard task, we evaluate the same user request in two versions of the marketplace (Figure 1 ). The matched control disables these mechanisms, while the incentive-misaligned condition activates all eight. The request, available products, product attributes, prices, availability, and user-optimal option remain identical across the two versions. The mechanisms change how the marketplace presents and mediates the same choice, including which products appear first, which receive sponsored or promotional treatment, when costs become visible, and what urgency or trust cues accompany them. Comparing optimal purchase rate across the two matched conditions measures the incentive-induced degradation defined in Section 2 . Benchmark settings. CAVEAT -Standard contains 52 tasks across the nine environments, with approximately 70 products in each scenario. We further construct CAVEAT -Hard to test the same decision problem at substantially larger search scale. Its 5 CAVEAT -Shop tasks each contain 2,112 products distributed across 88 result pages. This setting tests whether agents can maintain decision quality when finding strong candidates requires much broader exploration of the marketplace. 4 Evaluating CUAs under Incentive Misalignment We evaluate CUAs on CAVEAT using the widely used BrowserUse harness Müller and Žunič (2024) , holding the agent harness fixed across model families. Our main evaluation covers five widely used model families on all 52 CAVEAT -Standard tasks under both matched conditions, with three repetitions per task. To examine how robustness changes with reasoning, model scale, and model generation, we evaluate additional configurations on CAVEAT -Shop while holding the environment and tasks fixed. We further evaluate the strongest configuration on the five CAVEAT -Hard tasks with ten repetitions each. 4.1 Incentives Sharply Degrade User-Optimal Purchasing Activating the marketplace steering mechanisms reduces optimal purchase rate on CAVEAT -Standard from 78.6% to 17.3%, a drop of 61.3 percentage points (Figure 3 A). The user request, catalog, product facts, prices, availability, and user-optimal option remain unchanged between the two conditions. This matched comparison therefore isolates how strongly the agents’ decisions change in response to the marketplace incentives surrounding the same purchasing problem. The effect is not concentrated in a small subset of models. All five model families decline under incentive misalignment (Figure 3 B), with drops ranging from 37.2 to 78.9 percentage points. Even GPT-5.6-Sol with low reasoning, the strongest model in this comparison, falls from 91.0% in the matched control to 53.8% under incentive misalignment. The same degradation also occurs when using a different agent harness paired with a dedicated CUA model. Using Fara1.5-27B with its native Fara harness on CAVEAT -Shop, we observe a drop from 81.7% in the matched control to 3.3% under incentive misalignment. Using the 20 tasks in CAVEAT -Shop, we further isolate each incentive family while disabling the other seven. With all mechanisms disabled, GPT-5.6-Sol-low makes the optimal purchase in 100% of episodes; activating sponsored placement alone reduces this to 63.3%, preferential ranking to 75%, and drip pricing to 83.3%, while the remaining five families produce smaller drops. Figure 3: Incentive misalignment sharply reduces optimal purchasing. (A) Across five model families and all 52 CAVEAT -Standard tasks, optimal purchase rate falls from 78.6% in the matched control to 17.3% under incentive misalignment. (B) The degradation is consistent across model families. All five configurations perform worse under incentive misalignment, with drops ranging from 37.2 to 78.9 percentage points. (C) On CAVEAT -Hard, GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning achieves 90.0% in the matched control and 0.0% under incentive misalignment. Error bars denote 95% Wilson confidence intervals. CAVEAT -Hard makes the separation between underlying task capability and robustness to incentives especially clear. GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning purchases the user-optimal product in 90.0% of matched-control episodes, showing that it can solve these large-catalog decisions when the steering mechanisms are absent. With the same requests and catalogs under incentive misalignment, it makes no optimal purchase across 50 episodes (Figure 3 C). Thus, even when the underlying decision problem is demonstrably solvable, marketplace incentives can still induce a complete loss of optimal purchasing in this setting. 4.2 Robustness Improves with Model Capability The controlled comparisons in Figure 4 show that robustness improves as models receive more reasoning, scale to stronger variants, and advance across generations. Reasoning produces the clearest gains. GPT-5.6-Sol rises from 51.7% optimal purchasing at low reasoning to 90.0% at high reasoning, while GPT-5.5 improves from 12.0% at low reasoning to 50% with medium or high reasoning. Additional inference-time reasoning can therefore recover a substantial share of the performance lost under incentive misalignment. Figure 4: Robustness improves with model capability. All panels evaluate CAVEAT -Shop Standard under incentive misalignment. (A) Increasing reasoning effort raises optimal purchase rate for GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6-Sol. (B) Within GPT-5.6, performance rises from Luna to Terra to Sol, while the tested GPT-5 scale variants remain at floor. (C) At low reasoning effort, robustness remains at floor through GPT-5, becomes measurable with GPT-5.5, and rises sharply with GPT-5.6-Sol. Scaling shows a similar upward trend within GPT-5.6. At the same low-reasoning setting, optimal purchase rate rises from 0.0% for Luna to 11.7% for Terra and 51.7% for Sol (Figure 4 B). The corresponding GPT-5 nano, mini, and main configurations remain at 0.0%, indicating that greater scale alone is insufficient in the older generation and that the gains from scaling become visible only in the newer family. Model generation shows the same broader progression. At low reasoning effort, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, and GPT-5 remain at floor, after which optimal purchase rate rises to 12.0% for GPT-5.5 and 51.7% for GPT-5.6-Sol (Figure 4 C). Together, these comparisons show that robustness to marketplace incentives is improving with reasoning, scale, and newer model generations. At the same time, it continues to lag the models’ ability to solve the corresponding purchasing decisions in matched controls. This gap motivates a closer examination of how agent behavior changes when marketplace incentives are present. 5 Where Incentive Misalignment Enters the Decision Process Section 4 shows that agents often solve a purchasing problem in the matched control but choose differently once marketplace incentives are introduced. We next examine where this sensitivity enters the decision process. We qualitatively review 200 randomly sampled trajectories from the user request through purchase while hiding the final success label, then use recurring behaviors to motivate targeted analyses. The review points to departures in how agents preserve the user’s preferences, decide when to stop searching, and handle information that remains uncertain or has been read incorrectly. These observations identify three places in the decision process where an incentive-bearing environment can gain leverage through salience, visibility, and information availability. 5.1 Objective Drift Observation. In several trajectories, agents begin with a faithful account of the user’s requirements and preferences but change their effective priorities while browsing. A highly rated product, a prominent feature, or another salient cue can lead the agent to favor one preference over another even when the user assigned them equal importance. We therefore test whether the comparison remains stable under a change that leaves the user objective unchanged. Targeted analysis and ablations. We construct matched requests with two explicitly equal-priority preferences and reverse only their order. The catalog, preference values, stated priorities, and user-optimal product remain fixed. Yet the selected product changes in all 25 matched pairs and systematically shifts toward the preference mentioned first. The agent therefore introduces a priority that the user did not specify. Diagnosis. We call this objective drift . In an incentive-misaligned environment, such instability gives recommendations, promotional framing, ratings, and other salient cues a route to change which parts of the user’s objective dominate the comparison. 5.2 Premature Search Closure Observation. Failed trajectories often settle on a product that satisfies the hard requirements after comparing only a small set of visible options. Successful runs search more broadly, although both successful and failed agents frequently state that they have searched enough. This suggests that stopping decisions are poorly calibrated to search coverage, which becomes consequential when the environment controls which alternatives appear early. Targeted analysis and ablations. We run a matched placement intervention across all five CAVEAT-Shop product types and four comparative-preference settings, with three repetitions per setting and 60 runs per condition. Holding the request, catalog, and product attributes fixed, we move a suboptimal product from its normal position to a sponsored position near the top of the results. Its visit rate rises from 45/60 to 60/60, but its purchase rate rises much more sharply from 0/60 to 48/60, indicating that prominence changes how the product is treated after it is seen. This dependence on early visibility becomes especially damaging when the optimum requires deeper search. On CAVEAT -Hard, all 50 GPT-5.6-Sol-high failures stop on page 1 of an 88-page catalog and purchase a valid but suboptimal option while the optimum remains buried. Diagnosis. We call this premature search closure . Any incentive-bearing environment that controls the ordering or prominence of alternatives can exploit such a stopping rule through ranking, recommendations, or placement. 5.3 Premature Commitment with Unresolved Evidence Observation. Some failures remain even after search has succeeded. In these runs, the user-optimal product enters the comparison but is later rejected because a decision-relevant fact is missing, misread, or incorrectly remembered. To separate these cases from failures of discovery, we examine non-optimal purchases in which the optimum appears before the final decision and trace why the agent excludes it. Targeted analysis and ablations. To separate evidence failures from search failures, we examine non-optimal runs in which the user-optimal product had already been found. We identify 23 cases where the agent subsequently excludes it because a decision-relevant fact is misread, forgotten, or judged incorrectly, most often by confusing list and payable prices. These cases span 19 model–task–condition settings, and 13 contain another repetition that succeeds when the decisive fact is handled correctly. Thus, the failure occurs after discovery and turns on how the agent resolves the evidence needed for comparison. This suggests that delaying a decision-relevant fact may be enough to exploit the same weakness, which we test with drip pricing, where the initially displayed price can omit charges revealed only later in the transaction. We activate only drip pricing on CAVEAT -Shop while disabling the other seven steering mechanisms. Across 60 runs with GPT-5.6-Terra at low reasoning effort, the agent makes 35 suboptimal purchases, all selecting the drip-priced promoted product. Because no ranking, sponsorship, or other steering mechanism is active, these results isolate delayed price information as sufficient to substantially disrupt the comparison. Diagnosis. We call this premature commitment with unresolved evidence . The failure occurs when missing, delayed, conflicting, or misread information is treated as settled before the agent has enough evidence to support it. An incentive-misaligned environment can exploit this weakness by controlling which facts appear early and which require additional inspection. 6 Mitigating Incentive-Induced Failures The three failures identified in Section 5 suggest concrete requirements for robust decision-making under incentive misalignment. To show these requirements are actionable, we operationalize them at inference time with CAVEAT -Harness, then use the same decision behaviors to post-train CAVEAT -27B so that a smaller model can execute them more reliably. 6.1 CAVEAT -Harness: Operationalizing the Diagnosis We address objective drift by asking the evaluated model to convert the user request into a structured task specification before browsing begins. The specification records the hard and comparative requirements together with only the priorities explicitly stated by the user, and we keep it fixed throughout the episode. We address premature search closure and premature commitment with unresolved evidence with an optional verification tool. Before purchase, the agent can use the tool to justify that search is sufficiently complete from evidence available in the marketplace and to check whether missing or conflicting facts could still change the comparison. CAVEAT -Harness uses only the user request and information obtained through ordinary browsing; it receives no benchmark answers, hidden catalog state, or incentive metadata. We compare the full harness with baseline BrowserUse and a prompt-only baseline that describes the same decision principles without adding the structured task specification or verification tool (Figure 5 A–B, each task tested with three repetitions). On CAVEAT -Shop, CAVEAT -Harness raises GPT-5.6-Terra-low from 11.7% optimal purchasing with BrowserUse to 66.7%, compared with 30.0% under prompting alone. On CAVEAT -Hard, it raises GPT-5.6-Sol-high from 0.0% to 80.0%, compared with 13.3% under prompting. We further ablate the two harness components on CAVEAT -Hard and find that structured objectives alone reach 6.7%, whereas the verification tool alone reaches 66.7%. Together with the 80.0% result from the full harness, this suggests that search and evidence verification account for most of the gain in this large-catalog setting. Our trajectory review also finds cases where simply making the verification tool available leads the model to search more broadly before invoking it, suggesting that the checkpoint can influence stopping behavior in addition to filtering the final decision. As a lightweight cross-environment check, we evaluate four CAVEAT -Stay tasks with three repetitions each. CAVEAT -Harness raises GPT-5.6-Terra-low from 16.7% to 50.0%, providing preliminary evidence that the inference-time intervention transfers beyond CAVEAT -Shop. We also measure the interaction cost of this additional robustness. CAVEAT -Harness requires 2.6 × \times as much runtime, 2.3 × \times as many steps, and 2.3 × \times as many tool calls as baseline BrowserUse. The improvement therefore comes partly from inducing more extensive search and verification, motivating more efficient stopping and verification strategies. We therefore ask whether post-training can make the model execute the same decision procedure more reliably over long browser trajectories, producing CAVEAT -27B. We train Qwen3.5-27B in two stages. First, we use supervised examples synthesized by GPT-5.6-Sol-low in a separate synthetic environment to teach the behaviors required by the harness, including preserving the task specification, using the verification tool, and producing valid browser actions. We exclude all CAVEAT environments, tasks, catalogs, products, and benchmark answers from this stage. Second, we roll out the resulting model on CAVEAT -Shop laptop development tasks and train on corrected actions at states reached by its own policy. This exposes the model to navigation errors and recovery states that static demonstrations do not cover well. We use GPT-5.6-Sol-low with CAVEAT -Harness to provide corrected targets. We evaluate on the 16 non-laptop CAVEAT -Shop tasks, with three repetitions per task. The original Qwen3.5-27B achieves 0.0% with BrowserUse and 4.2% with CAVEAT -Harness, whereas CAVEAT -27B reaches 22.9% under the same harness (Figure 5 C), an 18.7 percentage-point gain over the untrained backbone. To test whether this improvement transfers beyond the training environment, we evaluate the same models on the four CAVEAT -Stay tasks. Qwen3.5-27B remains at 0.0% with either BrowserUse or CAVEAT -Harness, while CAVEAT -27B with the harness reaches 16.7%, providing preliminary evidence that post-training improves the model beyond CAVEAT -Shop. 7 Related Work Computer-use and shopping agents. Web and computer-use benchmarks evaluate navigation, tool use, and task completion across increasingly realistic interfaces Zhou et al. (2024) ; Deng et al. (2023) ; Xie et al. (2024) . Shopping benchmarks extend this setting to product search, recommendation, personalization, and complex user requests Yao et al. (2022) ; Ling et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) , while preference-following evaluations study whether agents infer and retain user preferences during interaction Zhao et al. (2025) ; Jiang et al. (2025) . CAVEAT goes beyond this by holding the underlying user decision fixed and varying the incentives shaping the environment, enabling end-to-end measurement of whether an agent preserves the user-optimal outcome under competing environmental incentives. Agent security and deceptive interfaces. Prior work studies web agents under prompt injection, malicious content, and other explicit attempts to redirect agent behavior Evtimov et al. (2026) ; Debenedetti et al. (2024) ; Zhan et al. (2024) , while recent benchmarks examine susceptibility to dark patterns and deceptive interfaces that alter ranking, presentation, or choice architecture Cuvin et al. (2026) ; Shi et al. (2026) ; Guo et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026) ; Bansal et al. (2025) . CAVEAT differs from this work in both what it varies and what it measures. It varies the environment’s incentives rather than introducing adversarial or deceptive content, instantiating a taxonomy of steering mechanisms in complete, high-fidelity marketplace environments. Every mechanism presents only accurate information, so the agent is never misled about the facts it needs to decide; the observed degradation arises from how agents respond to the ordering, salience, and timing of true information. And rather than scoring whether an agent avoids a particular pattern, CAVEAT scores whether it selects the user-optimal option from a full catalog with a verifiable optimum, exposing decision-level failures such as premature search closure that pattern-level scoring cannot observe. Platform incentives and consumer choice. Work in economics, recommender systems, and human–computer interaction has examined how platform objectives shape ranking, recommendation, sponsored placement, interface design, and consumer choice Xu et al. (2022) ; Mathur et al. (2019) ; Athey and Ellison (2011) . This literature motivates the incentive taxonomy instantiated in CAVEAT . By embedding these incentives in interactive environments with verifiable user-optimal outcomes, we study how autonomous agents mediate the resulting conflict between users and platforms, and whether the diagnosed failures can be mitigated. 8 Limitations and Future Work Our study focuses on online marketplaces, where CAVEAT can precisely control user-optimal outcomes and environmental incentives; extending the same methodology to domains such as financial services, hiring, or information platforms would test how broadly the observed failure modes transfer. CAVEAT also uses well-specified objectives with unique optima, providing clean causal measurement while leaving open richer settings with partial, evolving, or non-unique preferences. The current environments instantiate fixed steering mechanisms, whereas real platforms may adapt their behavior to the agent over time, motivating interactive and strategic extensions. Finally, the robustness gains from CAVEAT-Harness come with greater interaction cost, and evidence that either CAVEAT-Harness or CAVEAT -27B generalizes beyond CAVEAT -Shop is currently limited to a small CAVEAT -Stay evaluation. Future work should characterize this robustness–efficiency tradeoff and test transfer across broader environments, mechanisms, and domains. 9 Conclusion We introduced incentive-misaligned environments as a setting for evaluating whether CUAs preserve the user’s objective when the environment benefits from different outcomes. We instantiated this setting in CAVEAT and found that activating realistic marketplace steering mechanisms reduces optimal purchase rate from 78.6% to 17.3% under matched decision problems. We traced this degradation to objective drift, premature search closure, and commitment with unresolved evidence, then showed that interventions derived from these failures substantially improve robustness through both inference-time structure and targeted post-training. Together, our results suggest that evaluating delegated agents should include how reliably they preserve user objectives when the environments in which they act have incentives of their own.
